info.title: Integrating Siliko Core into Your Program

article.para: Siliko Core provides an interface to integrate parsing and evaluating mathematical expressions into a program. A developer can use the simple infix parser with the built-in set of functions to provide basic functionality, or write their own parser for another syntax, or add additional, custom functions to the lnguage.

section.para: Each header file is associated with a component of Siliko Core, such as in-language functions, the lexer, parser, and so on. In the API Reference each type and function lists which header it requires. For convenience, SilikoCore/SilikoCore.h includes all other public headers

info.title: The Parsing Pipeline and the Engine

section.para: Siliko Core uses a pipeline of components to parse input, then an engine to evaluate the the resulting syntax tree. The parsing pipeline goes through three components: a SilikoInput which is responsible for reading characters from some source of text to parse, a SilikoLexer which is responsible for converting the input characters into meaningful values and symbols, and the SilikoParseInfix function which is responsible for converting the sequence of symbols and values to an evaluatable parse tree.

The engine (a SilikoEngine object) is responsible for evaluating the syntax tree, and managing the lookup of functions that might be used during the evaluation. In the end, The result is given as a SilikoValue object which may be an integer, a real number, or an error.
If you wish, you can implement your own input source, parser, or use a different set of functions with the engine, including adding your own functions.

To provide input to a parser, you must build a SilikoInput object that Siliko Core’s lexical analyzer can use to read input text. To keep the input as versitle as possible, Siliko Core allows you to construct your own SilikoInput behavior to allow for various and disparate sources, such as a objects of a GUI library’s custom string type, network connections, files, or anything else that might be developed.
Siliko Core provides an SilikoInput implementation that takes a C string as its source.

The SilikoStringInputCreate function will copy the string passed to it, and build a new SilikoInput object that will read characters from the copied string. Other than calling this unique function, the resulting SilikoInput object is the same as any one made with a custom process.

A SilikoInput has two importantant pieces. First, it has a state object. This is what you use to keep track of what position you are in, which resources you are using, and so on. This should be a custom structure that you arrange however you need to fit your custom input. The second is a SilikoInputVTable which is a table of three function pointers that act on the state object.

The advance pointer points to a function that is used to advance the input stream by one character. The getCharacter pointer points to a function that returns the current character from the input stream, and the destroy pointer points to a function that cleans up and deletes the state object when the input is no longer needed.

Siliko Core’s lexical analyzer expects inputs to provide a sequence of characters. Since the lexical analyzer occasionally needs to read the current character multiple times, it uses separate advance and getCharacter functions to move forward in the sequence, and read the current character respectively.

The advance function should move to the next character in the input source, if possible, and must return true if there are more characters to read, and must return false if the input has been exhausted.

The getCharacter function returns the current character in the sequence. Since the lexical analyzer may call this function an unspecified number of times between calls to the advance function, the getCharacter function must be idempotent. Once the advance function returns false, indicating the end of input, the getCharacter function’s return value must be the null character, '\0'.

The destroy function must free up any resources used by the state object including deallocating the state object itself. So, if the state object was allocated with malloc, the state object should be passed to the free function. If the state object was allocated with a platform-specific allocation function, the destroy must use the appropriate deallocation function to free up the state object.

Siliko Core’s built-in lexical analyzer, SilikoLexer reads characters from a SilikoInput object, groups them into lexemes and produces a series of tokens from those lexemes. For more detail on the process see On Parsing.

info.title: How the Lexical Analyzer Processes Input

section.para: The lexical analyzer recognizes the following as single-character lexemes: +, -, *, /, ^, ,, (, ). When the lexical analyzer encounters any one of these characters, it stops processing and yeilds a single-character token matching the lexeme. The lexical analyzer also optionally recognizes d as a single-character operator, but will look at the next character to make sure it’s not part of a name before yielding a token.

The lexical analyzer will optionally recognize the lexemes e and pi as real numbers, and yield real-number tokens representing their values. A parser using the lexical analyzer with this enabled will not see any difference between these lexemes, and their same values entered manually.

Beyond these, the lexer recognizes a sequence of chatacters, starting with a letter as an ID, a sequence of numeric digits without a decimal point as an integer, and a sequence of numeric digits, including a single decimal point, as a real number.

Once you have a functioning SilikoInput oobject. The first step to using Siliko Core’s lexical analyzer is to set one up with the SilikoLexerCreate function. Its arguments are a pointer to a a SilikoInput object, and two boolean arguments representing whether to support the d operator, and whether to support the e and pi constants.
section.programlisting: SilikoInput *src = SilikoStringInputCreate("3d6"); SilikoLexer *lexer = SilikoLexerCreate(src, true, true);
section.para: After that point, if SilikoLexerCreate returned a non-null value, the SilikoLexer object was taken ownership of the passed SilikoInput object, and you must not pass the SilikoInput to SilikoInputDestroy.

info.title: Getting Tokens from the Lexical Analyzer

section.para: you can use the SilikoLexerGetToken function to get the current token. Once SilikoLexerAdvance is called, any pointers to previous SilikoToken objects are invalidated, so do any processing of the token before calling SilikoLexerAdvance and don’t call SilikoTokenDestroy on any tokens you get from SilikoLexer. The SilikoLexer object will take care of that.
If you write a parser using SilikoLexer, you can build it using any techniques requiring one token of look ahead.

The final piece in the built-in parsing pipeline is the SilikoParseInfix function. Which parses input in the Siliko infix language. It takes a pointer to a SilikoInput object, and returns a pointer to a SilikoNode object representing the root node of the syntax tree the parser generated.

Siliko implements syntax trees with the SilikoNode type. A SilikoNode can hold one of two kinds of data, a branch, or a leaf. A leaf has a single SilikoValue object, and a branch has a function call, and an array of child SilikoNode objects representing the arguments to the operation or function the branch represents.
There are six functions that will create a SilikoNode:

listitem.para: SilikoNodeCreateFromInteger generates a leaf node with an integer value.
SilikoNodeCreateFromReal generates a leaf node with a real-number value.
SilikoNodeCreateFromError generates a leaf node representing an error.
SilikoNodeCreateFromValue generates a leaf node by copying a SilikoValue.
SilikoNodeCreateBranch generates a branch node, taking the function name as its argument. Child nodes may be added afterward.

SilikoNodeCreateNothing generates a null node. This is used to represent when a parser component reports that is has no more to process or that it didn’t receive any tokens representing the rule that it handles, but this is not considered an error.

section.para: Each of these functions returns a pointer to a SilikoNode that will subsequently need to be passed to SilikoNodeDestroy to release resources. If you pass a branch node to SilikoNodeDestroy, it will also handle any child nodes the branch node has.

Each branch node keeps track of a list of children from left to right. For some functions, the order of the child nodes doesn't matter; 2 + 5 (or add(2, 5)) and 5 + 2 (or add(5, 2)) are effectively equivalent. However, for others, the order matters; 5 - 3 (or subtract(5, 3)) and 3 - 5 (or subtract(3, 5)) are not equivalent. So, the ‘Left’ functions will add the new child to the beginning of the list, while the ‘Right’ functions add to the end of the list. The functions with ‘Copy’ will make a copy of the new child and leave the original to the calling function to clean up, while the functions without will add the node passed directly to the branch node, taking ownership of the object.

Siliko Core uses SilikoEngine to look up functions such as sin and abs. This function lookup mechanism is also how arithmetic operations such as addition (+) and exponentiation (^) are handled. To create a new SilikoEngine object, use the SilikoEngineCreate function.

A new engine has no functions in its lookup table. Siliko Core provides two built-in sets of functions, one set implements the basic operators used by the built-in infix parser, and the other is a set of typical math functions included in C’s math.h header.
Use the function SilikoInstallOperations to install the functions required for the infix parser’s operator handling. This installs these functions:
Use the function SilikoInstallMathFunctions to install the functions that provide access to functions from C’s math.h header. Siliko Core provides support for these functions:

Both of these functions take a pointer to a SilikoEngine object, and return a bool indicating whether it was able to install all of the functions it’s supposed to install or not. A false return value indicates that a memory error occured. When this happens, the list of available functions in the function caller is unspecified.

If you wish to implement your own function, it needs to be installed to the function caller with the SilikoEngineInstallFunction function. The function takes a string representing the name of the function used within the Siliko language, and a SilikoFunction object implementing the the function.

The function SilikoEngineCallFunction takes a SilikoEngine, a function name as a C-style string, an argument count, and a pointer to the first element in an array of SilikoValue pointers. The engine finds the implementation for the function, then passes the argument count and argument array to the implementation, and returns the result returned by the implementation.
When you are finished with the SilikoEngine, pass it to the SilikoEngineDestroy function.

Once a syntax tree is fully assembled, it can be evaluated with the SilikoEvaluate function. The function takes two arguments: a SilikoEngine pointer, and a SilikoNode pointer. The engine will need to have any functions referenced by the syntax tree installed. If the engine fails to find a function name used, it will yield a SilikoErrorFunctionName error indicating that it failed to find a function.

The SilikoCore/Value.h header contains three types. The SilikoValue type represents a value passed to and yielded by the Siliko Core library. The SilikoValueStatus enumeration represents which type of value a SilikoValue holds: an integer (SilikoValueInteger), a real number (SilikoValueReal), or an error (SilikoValueError). The SilikoError enumeration represents an error that Siliko Core can encounter while parsing or evaluating expressions, for example a syntax error (SilikoErrorSyntax) or a division by zero error (SilikoErrorZeroDivision). For a full list of error values, see The SilikoError entry in the API Reference.
To make a SilikoValue object, you can use the functions, SilikoValueCreateFromInteger, or SilikoValueCreateFromReal. These functions take a long long int, and double, respectively.

You can use the SilikoValueGetStatus function to determine what type of value a SilikoValue holds. Then, based on which type it has, you can use one of SilikoValueGetError, SilikoValueGetInteger, or SilikoValueGetReal to retrieve the value.
In the tutorial program, the SilikoValue object returned by the parser was simply printed. In a more complex scenario, one might imagine using programming logic based on the value of a SilikoValue.
And finally, as we see in this example, when you are done with a SilikoValue you must call SilikoValueDestroy on the SilikoValue to avoid memory leaks.
